title: Hubble image of the Ring Nebula (Messier 57)
caption: The Ring Nebula, Messier 57, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: M 57, Messier 57, NGC 6720, Ring Nebula · constellation Lyra · about 2500 light-years away (source figure)
credit: NASA, ESA, and C. Robert O’Dell (Vanderbilt University).

recognition.text: Ranked #56 on ESA/Hubble’s published “Top 100 Images” list (an institutional selection, not an audience score).

story: Hubble captures the form and colours of the Ring Nebula, also known as Messier 57. The Ring is a planetary nebula, made of the cast-off outer layers of a dying star and lit up by the hot core left behind.

From Earth, the Ring looks like a simple ellipse with a ragged edge. Its real shape is more interesting. By combining existing ground-based data with new Hubble observations, astronomers discovered that the nebula has the form of a warped doughnut. Slotted into the doughnut's central gap is a rugby-ball-shaped region of thinner material, stretching toward and away from us.

The ring is a trick of perspective. We see a three-dimensional object squashed onto the flat sky, so a doughnut viewed nearly end-on can pass for a ring. Only by piecing together different observations can astronomers work out the true form. Hubble used a wide range of filters, each isolating light from a particular element, which helps reveal how gas is arranged throughout the nebula.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (2.10 x 2.10 arcminutes) and distance (2500 light years), the frame spans roughly 1.5 × 1.5 light-years. Its light set out about 2,500 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This visible-light image comes from Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3, using many narrow filters that isolate light from hydrogen, helium, oxygen, nitrogen and sulphur. The source does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: The narrow filters separate the light of individual elements in a way the eye cannot, and long exposures record gas far too faint to see directly.
